Hi everyone!

We've been working on the project Riemann dynamics, which aims to formalize important theorems in geometry, complex dynamics, and Teichmüller theory. As of now, we've successfully formalized the Uniformization Theorem, the No Wandering Domain Theorem, and the Measurable Riemann Mapping Theorem in Lean, downstream of Mathlib v4.29.0, RMT4, and Carleson. Each of the theorems formalized is sorry-free, and depends only on the three standard Lean axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). So far on the lean-eval website, we are the only submitted solution to the uniformization problem.

We would love to contribute parts of this to mathlib, and want to ask if mathlib would eventually want any of the theorems above. We are aware that it's better to contribute little by little, and since we've built all the prerequisites for stating and proving these theorems, there are two contributions that we are thinking can be added to mathlib directly right now.

  1. Wirtinger derivatives (PR #42630) — ∂/∂z\partial/\partial z∂/∂z and ∂/∂zˉ\partial/\partial\bar z∂/∂zˉ defined from fderiv ℝ, with the Cauchy–Riemann characterization (holomorphic ↔ ∂f/∂zˉ=0\partial f/\partial\bar z = 0∂f/∂zˉ=0) and product/chain/conjugation rules. ~260 lines depending only on existing Mathlib, as a new file Mathlib/Analysis/Complex/Wirtinger.lean beside RealDeriv.lean and Conformal.lean.

  2. The Riemann sphere as a complex manifold — ChartedSpace ℂ (OnePoint ℂ) and IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ) ω (OnePoint ℂ) instances via the two standard charts, as Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/Instances/RiemannSphere.lean.

Please let us know what you think, and we are happy to do additional cleaning so that everything complies with Mathlib's code standard.

I'm glad that you solved my uniformization challenge and continue to develop quasiconformal mappings and Teichmüller Theory!
Regarding the Riemann sphere, it has been defined twice, by @Geoffrey Irving in the ray repo, and by @Kenneth Shum's group with the paper Formalizing Extended Complex Numbers, Möbius Transformations, and Cross Ratio in Lean 4 (link to repo). However, I think a more principled approach would be realizing it as the complex projective line CP^1, which is itself a special case of #mathlib4 > Grassmannians @ 💬. This also makes the action of Möbius transformations (PSL(2,C)) easier using Quotient.lift and alike.

As an aside, I'm bit confused why the LeanEval challenge for connectedness of Mandelbrot set was only solved on July 22 after it was added on May 28/29, given that it's already solved in the ray repo.

Hi Junyan, thanks for getting back to us and for the feedback on the Riemann sphere!

We will hold off on a Riemann sphere PR for now and will follow the Grassmannian discussion. We will keep you posted on future PRs. After Riemann sphere is settled, we think adding quasiconformal mappings, basic vocabulary in complex dynamics, like Julia and Fatou sets, would be natural next additions for Mathlib.

I also had the same confusion for connectedness of Mandelbrot set, but my hypothesis is that lean-eval is a submission-based platform. So if someone formalizes a theorem but does not submit, then there's no official record on the benchmark.
Is the MRMT part usable as a dependency now, or is it heading for mathlib?

Hi Guanghao, MRMT is currently usable as a dependency. You can use it by adding our RiemannDynamics repo as a dependency. We were thinking of eventually upstreaming it to mathlib, but I don't think that will be possible in the near term.
Could beurling_lp_bound expose its constant? The 2^9 in eLpNorm_czOperator_beurling gets lost.

Hi Guanghao, the constant is (1/π) · beurlingTruncLpConst p for 1 < p < 2 (the real-interpolation constant from LpLow.lean), 1 at p = 2, and the same expression at the conjugate exponent for p > 2. The 2⁹ doesn't appear in it: it's only used to check the L² hypothesis (≤ C_Ts 4 = 2⁶⁴) that Carleson's CZ lemmas require. We didn't expose the constant since nothing downstream needs more than finiteness.
Has anyone already formalized A new proof of no-wandering domain theorems without quasiconformal techniques?
Lasse Rempe has generalised this to entire functions, and autoformalized that paper IIUC.
And they are on Zulip now!

Michael Rothgang said:

Lasse Rempe has generalised this to entire functions, and autoformalized that paper IIUC.

The formalisation is here:
https://palomar-registry.org/entry?id=PALOMAR-2026-09-25-000001&version=1

It is going to be a big mess though because it was auto-formalised; I think the rational case, or indeed the case of finitely many singular orbits - where the argument is very simple - may be worth its own formalisation. Here the argument comes down to the classical fact that the hyperbolic area of the sphere with k+2 punctures is 2kpi (which is something that was formalised as part of the project). Note that the bounded-orbit wandering domain absence was since also announced in preprints by Drach--Pardo-Simón--Učakar, and by Ye.

Hello Will,

We (the complex dynamics group in Manchester) is also very interested in formalising one-dimensioanl holomorphic dynamics and getting this into Mathlib / perhaps first Tau Ceti in a clean form. Should we join forces? Perhaps this thread could be a useful place to co-ordinate for those who are interested.

One question is what would be a good setting for the most general definitions. My suggestion would be: X is a Riemann surface, U is an open subset of X, and f\colon U\to X is an open (=nowhere locally constant) holomorphic function. [One can discuss whether X should required to be connected, or whether it could also be a (not necessarily connected) one-dimensional complex manifold.] Of course, various theorems will require more, but in what I understand to be the spirit of mathlib, might this be the most general setting in which to define the basic objects such as Fatou and Julia sets.

Of course, for Fatou and Julia sets, we could be evern more general: Normality makes sense on any open subset of a compact Hausdorff space. (Here: The one-point compactification of the surface X, if it is not compact itself.) Indeed, every such space has a unique uniformity compatible with the topology, and notions like equicontinuity and locally uniform convergence make sense then. So one could define Fatou and Julia sets in this generality, although obviously once complex analysis results come into it, one should specialise to spaces with a complex structure - hence the suggestion above.

Would be happy to hear everyone's thoughts!

Hi Lasse, congratulations on your recent work! After talking to my collaborators at Cornell, we’d be very interested in joining forces. It would be great to discuss further how we can coordinate and eventually upstream the definitions and theorems in complex dynamics into mathlib.

Also, thank you for raising the question of generality. This is also my understanding of mathlib, that it wants definitions to be at an appropriate level of generality, with additional hypotheses introduced later in the specific theorems. Currently, our Riemann Dynamics repo has developed a lot of basic definitions and theorems in complex dynamics. I think some of them are already in good shape, but others can be made more general for incorporation into mathlib. 

For example, IsNormal already only takes an arbitrary topological domain and a uniform-space codomain. But our current definitions of Julia set and Fatou set, as defined here, are only for self maps of the Riemann sphere. For mathlib purposes, I agree that they should be extended to a general Riemann surface.

Guanghao Li said:

Thanks Will, that clears it up. Finiteness is enough for what I need right now: I'm using MRMT as a dependency for a Kneser tetration formalization. If I ever need explicit bounds, I'll unfold beurlingTruncLpConst myself, or send a small PR to expose it, if you'd accept one. Also, Rempe's no-wandering-domain work looks relevant here, so I'll keep an eye on that too.

Hi Guanghao, I’m glad that you find our work useful! You’re welcome to submit a PR to Riemann Dynamics. Good luck with your formalization!

Thank you Will - yes, that sounds good to me to have normality as a definition for families taking values in a uniform space; in fact, that is how it was also formalised in my projects (although there it was formalised just for sequences, rather than full families of functions, with the latter obviously the correct setting). Then for a map on a subset of a complex 1-manifold $X$, the set of normality is the set of normality of the iterates with respect to the uniformity of the one-point compactification of X. (I think it doesn't really matter if X is already compact.) One note: There is a difference here between the set of normality and the Fatou set, which also should contain points that map outside the closure of the domain of definition (a condition that is stable under perturbation).

I think Riemann surfaces are not currently in Mathlib, although complex manifolds are, so this is probably straightforward.

As a note, the results about absence of bounded-orbit wandering domains all work in this general setting.

Hi Lasse, thanks for clarifying the distinction. I agree these would be good definitions for the set of normality and the Fatou set in mathlib. Also, to my understanding, it's good to make small additions to mathlib each time. Specifically, I think once there's agreement here on the definitions/theorems, it might be a good idea to start submitting small PRs.

Will (Ziang) Li said:

Hi Lasse, thanks for clarifying the distinction. I agree these would be good definitions for the set of normality and the Fatou set in mathlib. Also, to my understanding, it's good to make small additions to mathlib each time. Specifically, I think once there's agreement here on the definitions/theorems, it might be a good idea to start submitting small PRs.

That is a good point - we should start to create some small PRs, and the definition of normality is a good starting point. We discussed this a bit in our working group this morning, and decided that there are a few things to clarify.

Normality is a condition about relative compactness. In particular, in the settings we are interested in, it is precisely the statement that a set of functions between two topological spaces is relatively compact in the compact-open topology. Here there is no need for any uniformity.

Now, for sufficiently general spaces, two things diverge: locally uniform convergence, and compactness versus sequential compactness.

In your definition, you use sequential compactness for the topology of locally uniform convergence. Is this the right definition? Or should it be actual compactness?

The two things are equivalent in locally compact spaces. This is already in Mathlib as ContinuousMap.tendsto_iff_tendstoLocallyUniformly; actually weakly locally compact (there exists at least one compact neighbourhood) is enough.

Two more quick comments:

  • I think I would broaden the definition of 1-dimensional holomorphic dynamical systems suggested above: We should not require the target X to be connected, but rather allow it to be a 1-dimensional compact manifold. This allows us to include the setting of Adam Epstein's finite type maps, where the range is a compact 1-manifold, but not necessarily connected.
  • Our maps are not globally defined necessarily. I know that there is a tendency in Mathlib to just extend such maps arbitrarily in an arbitrary way, but mathematically I would prefer to use "local" maps, defined on open subsets of the target space X. The current formalisation of the bounded-orbit result uses such a definition, although it is undoubtedly not very clean at this point.

Hi Lasse, we discussed your proposed definitions in our meeting yesterday. We agree that your definition for normal families is more general in not requiring the target to be a uniform space, and we think this would be a good definition for mathlib. We especially like your points about the maps not necessarily being globally defined, since this can be useful in a lot of cases.

Will (Ziang) Li said:

Hi Lasse, we discussed your proposed definitions in our meeting yesterday. We agree that your definition for normal families is more general in not requiring the target to be a uniform space, and we think this would be a good definition for mathlib. We especially like your points about the maps not necessarily being globally defined, since this can be useful in a lot of cases.

Thank you Will! There is at least one point to discuss: Should normality already allow the limit functions to take the value infinity? That is, is normality of a family of functions X->Y relative compactness in the space of functions X-> Y, or in the space of functions X -> one-point compactification of Y? The latter is really what we want in our applications. On the other hand, Ahlfors for example also allows considering just the topology of the plane, in which case functions converging uniformly to infinity are ruled out.

Currently, I tend towards using the one-point compactification, but would value other views.

The other question is to be consistent with definitions already in the literature, as much as possible. I asked ChatGPT to do a search, and it seems that there isn't much beyond one complex variable, and what there is isn't necessarily consistent. One key setting is complex manifolds (Wu, Normal families of holomorphic mappings, Acta Math 1967). Here, there is a key subtlety: Wu does not allow convergence to functions that take the value infinity at some points, but not at others. In one complex variable, if the domain is connected, then this is automatic, but not in several variables, it seems. (Take maps from the disc to \C^2, f_n(z) = (1/z, 1/n) for a stupid example.)

My tendency would be that our definition of normality is the more natural for general topological spaces; the normality in higher-dimensional complex manifolds, if it is eventually introduced, would then be a different notion, maybe "Wu normality". What do you think? This should be clearly documented, I think.

Other definitions are:

  • in the case of quasiregular mappings, Fletcher–Nicks, Normal families and quasiregular mappings, Definitions 2.13 and 3.3, which I think is quite close to ours;
  • Beardon and Minda (Normal families: a geometric perspective) also discuss normality, but here use metric properties of the hyperbolic metric - I don't think that this is necessarily suited to the general definition we want in Mathlib;
  • Infinite-dimensional holomorphy: Kim–Krantz, Normal families of holomorphic functions and mappings on a Banach space, Definition 1.4 and §6. According to ChatGPT, this uses the compact-open topology, but with respect to the weak-* topology on the target space, so it would somewhat fit with our definition, but I haven't actually looked at the paper or considered the ramifications myself.

Right now, my suggestion would be to agree whether or not the definition should involve one-point compactification, and then prepare to make a pull request. My PhD student @Filip Moruś has also been looking at writing Lean, and might be happy to discuss a proposed coding of the definition.

Hi Lasse, thanks for taking the lead and pushing this forward! Personally, I'm also leaning towards using the one-point compactification, since this is also more suitable for our Riemann Dynamics project. I also agree that for "Wu normality," we can discuss and introduce later if needed.

Here's a draft for the normal family definition in Lean that I wrote. 

import Mathlib.Topology.Compactification.OnePoint.Basic
import Mathlib.Topology.CompactOpen

def IsNormalFamily {X Y : Type*}
    [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
    (F : Set C(X, OnePoint Y)) : Prop :=
  IsCompact (closure F)

Feel free to use or adapt this for the PR. Alternatively, I'd be happy to make the PR and add you, Filip, and other members of your group as collaborators on the PR.
Hello Will, that sounds great - I'm very happy to be a collaborator on the PR; @Filip Moruś also, I believe.
Sounds good! Please let me know the email addresses that you and Filip want to use.
Hi Lasse and Filip, I’ve opened mathlib PR #45111 with the normal-family definition we discussed, using the one-point compactification. Thanks again for the discussion!

This definition is probably not optimal. Let me explain. I can envision two use cases:

  • Either you are considering functions with values in ℂ, and you want to say when they form a normal family. Then, to apply your definition, you would first need to compose your functions with the inclusion from ℂ to the sphere, which would make it slightly inconvenient. Better have a definition akin to "A family of functions to ℂ is normal if their composition with the map to the sphere has compact closure"
  • Or you are going to work from the start with functions taking values in the sphere. But then the fact that the sphere is a one-point compactification shouldn't be relevant, and you should then talk about a normal family in any topological space, not only one point compactifications.

Which of the two choices is good for you can only depend on your applications. My advice would be to develop more than just one definition: build your library until the proof of the first interesting theorem, and then it will inform you of what definitions are good. Don't do it directly as PRs to Mathlib, though: do it as a project downstream of Mathlib, and once it is mature enough to prove that your definitions work well, then you can start PRing stuff to Mathlib if you like.

Thank you @Sébastien Gouëzel for the suggestions. The idea of developing more of a project sounds like a good one.

However, I would like to clarify one thing about the proposed definition; which some thought has gone into. I think that you misunderstood the role of the one-point compactification in the definition; it is not primarily related to the question of the complex plane versus the Riemann sphere.

The idea is not to consider only holomorphic families of functions in the plane or the sphere; indeed here just having a definition for maps to the sphere would be enough. As you will see if you look further up in the conversation, the general setting would be for maps to one-dimensional complex manifolds. Normality usually allows divergence to infinity, which is why we included the one-point compactification.

It is true that in most applications, the functions will naturally take values in a compact one-dimensional manifold. And working with the one-point compactification of such a compact manifold is indeed cumbersome, so there would need to be a proposition that says that, in this case, the given notion of normality is the same as relative compactness in the compact-open topology of the target.

However, the basic definitions make sense also when the target is e.g. an infinite-genus surface, and at least one recent result (absence of bounded-orbit wandering domains) holds in this general setting. So I think that whatever definitions go into Mathlib should allow for this generality, and I tend to think that it would be cleaner to have the "right" definition that gives the right results in the desired generality, rather than having a definition of e.g. Fatou set / set of normality that depends on whether the target manifold is compact or not.

Still, your point about developing the project a bit further before making mathlib PRs is taken. @Will (Ziang) Li , would it make sense to make a new separate GitHub project to which we may add things from our existing projects as appropriate? It may also be good to make a "roadmap" that could be submitted to Tau Ceti. I don't have any experience with this, but it would be good to look into this (or possibly ask AI to look into creating such a roadmap). The key would be to audit definitions formally - we can continue to use this thread for the discussion?

A first suggestion at what we would want:

  • The definition of normality
  • The definition of a one-dimensional complex dynamical system. (Suggestion: It consists of a complex one-manifold XXX, an open subset OOO of XXX and an open holomorphic function ϕ ⁣:O→X\phi\colon O\to Xϕ:O→X.
  • The definition of key sets: the set of normality \Omega(f) (largest open subset on which the iterates are all defined and form a normal family / all points that have an open neighbourhood on which iterates are defined and form an open family); the non-absconding set (points where all iterates are defined) and absconding set (points that eventually map to a point in the complement of O); the stably absconding set (points that eventually map to a point outside the closure of the domain of definition); the pre-boundary set (points that eventually map to a point on the boundary; i.e. absconding but not stably absconding); the Fatou set (union of normality set and stably absconding set); the Julia set (complement of the Fatou set in XXX).
  • The definition of key classes of 1d complex ds: rational maps on the Riemann sphere, transcendental entire functions, transcendental meromorphic functions, finite-type maps in the sense of Epstein, Ahlfors islands maps in the sense of Epstein.

How does that sound? This is only the starting point, so it would be good to get a working version of these definitions that we are happy with. There are various next steps that might be pursued after that:

  • Basic results about normal families. I think you already formalised quite a bit of normal families including Montel's theorem in RiemannDynamics, so we could look at including those statements, adapted to the above definitions, in a Tau Ceti roadmap? I think that you formalised Montel's theorem using the universal covering of the thrice-punctured sphere. My favourite route is different: using Zalcman's rescaling principle, which is a generally important principle that is also used in what I think is the easiest proof of density of repelling periodic points for rational maps / transcendental entire functions. This also gives Picard's theorem at the same time. I think Zalcman's lemma is already in your library, correct? There is also a library of complex dynamics and complex analysis results that have been auto-formalised in my work; I should ask AI to clean this up sometime and share it with the others collaborating on this project, probably.
  • Key properties of the Julia set, e.g. it is non-empty and infinite (for interesting maps such as the classes mentioned above). For transcendental entire functions, this already needs Picard's theorem, though.
  • Density of repelling periodic points for the classes in question. The best route is through Zalcman, I believe, for the classical function classes. For finite-type maps, it follows from the result for Ahlfors islands maps, which directly uses the Ahlfors islands property. Of course, at some point, one should prove that transcendental entire and meromorphic functions are Ahlfors islands maps, which requires the Ahlfors islands theorem. There is a proof by Bergweiler using qc mappings and (you guessed it) Zalcman rescaling. In fact, for density of repelling periodic points, I think the qc mappings part is not required; a weaker version of the islands property is sufficient. The classical proof, of course, is via an extension of value distribution theory. @Stefan Kebekus has been formalising Nevanlinna theory - I assume that the Ahlfors theory of covering surfaces might be some way off, however?

Sorry, this has become a longer post than I had intended. I will leave it here for now - please let me know any comments!

Sure, I get that. Still, I think the definition you have written is not the right one, for usability reasons, and you should choose between the two alternatives I have given. It's not for mathematical reasons, it's really a formalization issue here.

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

Lasse Rempe said:

However, I would like to clarify one thing about the proposed definition; which some thought has gone into. I think that you misunderstood the role of the one-point compactification in the definition; it is not primarily related to the question of the complex plane versus the Riemann sphere.

Sure, I get that. Still, I think the definition you have written is not the right one, for usability reasons, and you should choose between the two alternatives I have given. It's not for mathematical reasons, it's really a formalization issue here.

I am not sure that I fully understand. Your definitions are for maps to the plane or the sphere, so they are not sufficiently general for our purposes. I was of the impression that the aim of Mathlib is to have the fundamental definitions phrased in the correct generality, so I am not sure what the benefit would be to define this only in the case of the plane.

Of course, there would likely be a proposition that says that, in the case of the plane, the definition is equivalent to both characterisations that you give. And one or the other could be the definition for "is a normal family of functions to \C".

But maybe I am missing the point. I thought that our definition was exactly "A family of functions to X is normal if their composition with the map to its one-point compactification has compact closure", which is what your Definition 1 says (specialised to the case of X=\C)? The second definition would correspond to just defining normality for families of functions taking values in a compact space. Then in the definition of the Fatou set, we would either apply this to the composition with the inclusion in the one-point compactification, or we would distinguish cases: if the target is already compact, we don't need to compose with the inclusion. Mathematically this does not seem the cleanest solution. Whether it would be easier for practice, I don't know. Another disadvantage is that this is not really consistent with existing usage.

EDIT. Ah, I think now I see. The problem is that our definition assumes that our functions already take values in the one-point compactification. That was indeed not what we had intended - it should have been "a family of functions to X is normal if their composition with the map to its one-point compactification has compact closure". Sorry for misunderstanding, and many thanks for pointing this out.

Would something like the below be an appropriate formalisation of the definition, in the sense discussed? Should we go forward with something like this?

public import Mathlib.Topology.Compactification.OnePoint.Basic
public import Mathlib.Topology.CompactOpen

@[expose] public section

/-- A family of continuous maps is normal if, after inclusion of the target into
its one-point compactification, it has compact closure in the compact-open topology. -/
def IsNormalFamily {X Y : Type*}
    [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
    (F : Set C(X, Y)) : Prop :=
  IsCompact (closure ((fun f : C(X, Y) ↦
    (⟨OnePoint.some ∘ f,
      OnePoint.continuous_coe.comp f.continuous⟩ :
      C(X, OnePoint Y))) '' F))
I have created a github repository at https://github.com/LR-UK/OneDimensionalComplexDynamics/ . Currently it only has the definition above.

Lasse Rempe schrieb:

  • Stefan Kebekus has been formalising Nevanlinna theory - I assume that the Ahlfors theory of covering surfaces might be some way off, however?

That's correct. At least at present, that part of the theory is out of scope for ProjectVD.

@Will (Ziang) Li @Filip Moruś I propose that we continue the discussion of basic definitions. Our notion of a one-dimensional dynamical system will require the notion of one-dimensional complex manifolds, and much of the project will surely require Riemann surfaces. In RiemannDynamics, I don't think that you provided explicit packaging as classes, but I would say that it makes sense to do this. The following would be potential definitions.

import Mathlib.Geometry.Manifold.Complex
import Mathlib.Data.PFun

open scoped Manifold

noncomputable section

class abbrev ComplexOneManifold (X : Type*) :=
  TopologicalSpace X, T2Space X, ChartedSpace ℂ X,
  IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ) 1 X

class abbrev RiemannSurface(X : Type*) :=
  ComplexOneManifold X, ConnectedSpace X

There are a few questions here.

  • I believe you used analytic regularity in RiemannDynamics, while here C^1 is proposed. Of course, the two are equivalent. There seem to be a number of places in Mathlib already where C^1 is used for complex manifolds, so this might be the preferred choice. In Tau Ceti there is a proposition that complex manifolds of any regularity are analytic (IsManifold.of_ne_zero), and analyticity of complex differentiable functions is in Mathlib as DifferentiableOn.analyticOnNhd. So maybe it doesn't matter so much which we choose - any thoughts?
  • Second countability is not required by the definition of a manifold, so with the above definitions, ComplexOneManifold and RiemannSurface do not assume second countability. We will mainly be concerned with compact complex one manifolds anyway, and Riemann surfaces are second countable by Radó's theorem. However, Radó's theorem is on Palomar (by @Rado Kirov ), but not on Tau Ceti or Mathlib, as far as I know. I am not sure whether there are any plans to add it to either?
  • Note that a ComplexOneManifold may be empty according to the above definition. Whether we want to allow this in the definition of a complex dynamical system is something we should discuss. A few comments on your tentative definition

/-- A family of continuous maps is normal if, after inclusion of the target into
its one-point compactification, it has compact closure in the compact-open topology. -/
def IsNormalFamily {X Y : Type*}
    [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
    (F : Set C(X, Y)) : Prop :=

I have hidden the definition, and only kept its type, because that's the first thing one should settle on. I see two ways to improve things.

The first is that you are using a family of continuous functions. This corresponds to the usual mathematical intuition, but in practice this will make things complicated, because you will need to provide continuity proofs whenever you use this definition. In practice, we have learnt in Mathlib that it's often more efficient to use unbundled objets, i.e., the type would be

def IsNormalFamily {X Y : Type*}
    [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
    (F : Set (X → Y) : Prop :=

The second is that you are using a definition on the whole type. When you want to say that a family of functions is normal on an open subset, say, then your idea is probably to compose your functions with the canonical inclusion from the open subset to the whole space, and say that this family of composed functions is normal. Mathematically, it definitely makes sense. From a formalization point of view, it means you need to juggle between functions defined on the whole space and functions defined on subtypes, and this creates lots of annoyance. Another lesson we have learnt in Mathlib is that, for this kind of predicates that are of a somewhat local nature, it's better to avoid the global definition, and instead have predicates IsNormalFamilyWithinAt, IsNormalFamilyAt, IsNormalFamilyOn and IsNormalFamily. That's what we do for continuity, differentiability, analyticity, and so on. The basic object would be IsNormalFamilyWithinAt, where IsNormalFamilyWithinAt F s x would say that there is a neighborhood of x within s on wich the family F is normal (which you may define with composing coercions as you like, or by giving a direct definition). And the other definitions would be built in terms of this one.

With these definitions, the Fatou set of a map is very easy to define, for instance: it is the set of points at which the family {f^[n]} is normal.

Dear @Sébastien Gouëzel thank you so much for taking the time to post this, it is incredibly helpful. I had wondered myself about whether or not to include continuity as a requirement, so given your comments here I agree that it may be better to remove this.

However, the compact-open topology is usually defined only for continuous functions, and when the limit functions are allowed to be discontinuous, it no longer agrees with uniform convergence on compact sets (even for compact spaces). So we would need to decide what the correct definition is when we allow discontinuous functions.

Your point about the local version of the definition also makes sense. However, the definition of normality that we settled on is (in this generality) not a local property. Of course, it is a local property in the cases where we apply it. So we would need to decide whether we want to replace it by a local property (which will be equivalent in the cases that we care about) for reasons of ease of coding, or whether there is some other way forward. Any thoughts from the others on this?

I have a question about the level of generality of the current definition. Would it be useful to impose additional assumptions on the domain $X$, at least when establishing the local–global equivalence? In the applications I have in mind, $X$ would be an open subset of $\mathbb{C}$, such as the open unit disc. Although normality on a singleton is meaningful, I am mainly interested in the behaviour of the family on a common neighbourhood of a point.

Could we keep the current definition and introduce a separate notion of normality at a point? We would say that a family$\mathcal{F}$ is normal at $p\in X$ if there exists an open neighbourhood $U_{p}$ of $p$ such that the restricted family $\mathcal{F}_{U_{p}}$ is normal in the current sense.

We could then try to establish, under the hypotheses relevant to our applications, that normality on $X$ is equivalent to normality at every point of $X$.

Yes, I am leaning in this direction also. Just one small remark on terminology: should it be normality "near" a point, rather than "at" a point? Unlike, for instance, continuity, this local notion also established normality near all points in a neighborhood. Our spaces will be locally compact and, usually, second countable.

(If we allow arbitrary complex 1-manifolds, these may not be second countable, but a) this should not cause any problems if the definitions are right, and b) these cases are not of interest in practice, so we can add second countability as an assumption if that becomes convenient.)

I wonder whether or not we should replace the compact open topology by locally uniform convergence, however. We can then have a lemma that says they are equivalent in certain circumstances (which will usually cover our use cases).

I agree with you that "near" would maybe be more natural mathematically. However, for coherence throughout Mathlib, we always use "at" for this kind of notion. For instance, ContDiffAt f 1 x (read "f is C^1 at x") really means that there is a neighborhood of x on which f is differentiable, with a continuous derivative. But still we name it using at. Same thing for AnalyticAt.

However, the compact-open topology is usually defined only for continuous functions, and when the limit functions are allowed to be discontinuous, it no longer agrees with uniform convergence on compact sets (even for compact spaces). So we would need to decide what the correct definition is when we allow discontinuous functions.

If you are only going to apply this to continuous functions, then what really matters is that your definition is the right one when your functions are continuous. The definition doesn't need to be interesting when the functions are not continuous, because all the good theorems will have a continuity assumption. In this kind of situation, what we try to do is pick the definition that does the right thing in the relevant case (here continuous functions), and moreover is so that as many results as possible still hold without the continuity assumption -- so that users of these theorems don't have the burden of proving continuity, even if their functions are continuous: saving time for your users is a very worthwile goal.
